claims.claim: He was born on 11 June 1990 at Guy's Hospital in London (FAQ and birth_date frontmatter); the body says only 'Born in London in 1990'.
claims.passage: He was born on June 11, 1990, at Guy's Hospital in London
claims.inference: Exact date from Wikipedia (S32) only; year and hospital from his own 2016 account (S06); Walthamstow from S07, S10 and S09. His stated ages (25 in March 2016, 29 in February 2020, 33 in August 2023, 35 in March 2026) all fit June 1990.
claims.alternative: None on the facts. If a primary source for the day cannot be found, the year alone is safe; never turn the year into 1 January.

claims.claim: Born in London in 1990; RSC's first Black Hamlet in 2016.
claims.passage: Essiedu became the Royal Shakespeare Company's first Black Hamlet in 2016
claims.inference: Orientation fact reported by The Sunday Times (2026) and Glass (2021); the 1990 London birth is his own 2016 account (S06).
claims.alternative: None on the facts.

claims.claim: He broke through on screen as Kwame in I May Destroy You (2020).
claims.passage: broke through on screen as Kwame in Michaela Coel's _I May Destroy You_ in 2020
claims.inference: Orientation; widely reported.
claims.alternative: "Broke through" is the draft's summary; The Sunday Times calls it his TV breakthrough.

claims.claim: His father, Tony, a lawyer, returned to Ghana when Essiedu was very young (sources conflict: 'a baby' vs 'four') and died when Essiedu was 14.
claims.passage: His father, Tony, a lawyer, went back to Ghana when Essiedu was very young and died when he was 14.
claims.inference: Repeated in his interviews across 2016-2026. Tony was 'popular, extrovert, a raconteur' and 'had not been an active father', but Essiedu 'felt his loss profoundly' (S01, journalist's paraphrase plus his quote about never making the relationship what he wanted).
claims.alternative: The age at which his father left conflicts between sources; write 'when he was very young' or attribute each version. Do not build a causal 'absent father' story; he does not draw one.

claims.claim: FAQ restatement of the father facts.
claims.passage: His father, Tony, a lawyer, returned to Ghana when Essiedu was very young
claims.inference: Same facts as C02, in FAQ metadata.
claims.alternative: Age at departure conflicts between sources; "very young" avoids choosing.

claims.claim: His mother, Selina, taught fashion and design at adult-education colleges, raised him alone on little money, pushed him academically, and died of breast cancer in his first year at Guildhall, when he was 20, after seven years with cancer that was never discussed with him as terminal.
claims.passage: She had cancer for seven years and died in his first year at the Guildhall School of Music and Drama, when he was 20.
claims.inference: Consistent across S01 (cancer for seven years, four months in hospital, 'at no point did we have a conversation ... about her dying'; 'she definitely protected me from that'), S04 (breast cancer at 20), S02 and S07 (her job).
claims.alternative: None on the facts. Her death year is about 2010 (first year at Guildhall, which he entered in 2009 per S25; S24 says 'the sadness that I felt in 2010'); avoid an exact date.

claims.claim: Selina taught fashion and design and raised him alone in Walthamstow.
claims.passage: His mother, Selina, who taught fashion and design at adult-education colleges, raised him alone in Walthamstow, east London.
claims.inference: Biographical; consistent across 2016, 2022 and 2024.
claims.alternative: None on the facts.

claims.claim: 'My mum was my best mate'; asked whether she knew she was dying: 'Maybe. Probably. But she definitely protected me from that.'
claims.passage: Maybe. Probably. But she definitely protected me from that.
claims.inference: Establishes what he said, to whom and when; it is a self-report, not proof of motive.
claims.alternative: Retrospective account; he notes it may "feel dumb retrospectively" that he did not know.

claims.claim: He held a place to study medicine at UCL before choosing drama school.
claims.passage: He had a place to study medicine at University College London.
claims.inference: Told consistently 2016-2024; the two-year audition detail and Guildhall being the last recall are from S25 (audio). S11 has the journalist's summary that he was rejected by all but one school.
claims.alternative: The age he won the scholarship is inconsistent (11 in S10; entered at seven in S12): omit it. He has said medicine was the expected route for 'the son of a West African woman' (S16) and that acting felt 'renegade', a choice he made rather than one made for him (S10).

claims.claim: Medicine as the expected route: 'you can be a doctor or you can be an accountant'.
claims.passage: you can be a doctor or you can be an accountant
claims.inference: Establishes what he said, to whom and when; it is a self-report, not proof of motive.
claims.alternative: A common, partly comic line about immigrant parents; context, not a type clue.

claims.claim: Acting felt 'renegade', 'a choice that I was making, as opposed to a choice that was being made for me'.
claims.passage: a choice that I was making, as opposed to a choice that was being made for me
claims.inference: Shows him framing the riskier route as his own choice; counterweight to a purely security-seeking reading.
claims.alternative: Glass is a fashion-culture magazine; promotional context.

claims.claim: His mother wanted him to have a secure profession but backed his drama-school attempt on condition he took it as seriously as medicine; he says her consent mattered greatly to him, and a half-sister later told him their mother privately counted each rejection as a step back toward medical school.
claims.passage: She knew how important her consent was to me
claims.inference: S01: 'She knew how important her consent was to me' and her instruction to treat acting with a doctor's professionalism 'was just what I needed to hear'. S06: her 'first-generation immigrant commitment to safety and success'. S25 (audio): the rejection consolation and the half-sister's later revelation. Suggests that a trusted authority's blessing and a safety frame were central to how he made the riskiest decision of his youth.
claims.alternative: Many children of immigrants seek a parent's approval for a risky career; this is context, not a type proof. The 'sly' detail in S25 is audio; paraphrase it.

claims.claim: His mother's condition for drama school, quoted by him.
claims.passage: You've got to treat it in the same way you would if you were a doctor, the same level of professionalism.
claims.inference: His mother's words as he recalls them; he says it "was just what I needed to hear".
claims.alternative: Reported speech of a deceased parent, recalled years later.

claims.claim: In 2016 he credited his mother with 'that first-generation immigrant commitment to safety and success'.
claims.passage: that first-generation immigrant commitment to safety and success
claims.inference: Establishes what he said, to whom and when; it is a self-report, not proof of motive.
claims.alternative: His description of her, not of himself.

claims.claim: Two years of auditions; Guildhall the last school to hold final recalls; a half-sister told him in 2024 that his mother rang her after each rejection, still hoping he would end up at medical school.
claims.passage: Only that year did his half-sister tell him that his mother used to ring her after each rejection, still hoping he would end up at medical school.
claims.inference: Paraphrase of an audio account (two transcriptions agree on the passage c.0:12:30-0:15:20). "Still hoping" summarises his framing that she was "nearly at the finish line" and keeping up "the pretense".
claims.alternative: Machine transcript; small.en hears "sly with it" where medium hears "slow with it", so no quotation is used. The half-sister is his father's daughter (S06), not Selina's, and the draft says "his mother".

claims.claim: Before almost every new job he goes through intense anticipatory dread that he will be exposed as not good enough, to the point of needing people close to him to get him to work on the first day; once the work starts it usually passes.
claims.passage: I need a lot of support from the people who are close to me to drag me into the car to go to work on that first day
claims.inference: S01 is the clearest statement ('on the day before the first day on every job, I have a nervous breakdown, thinking: this is the one where people will find me out'; 'I need a lot of support from the people who are close to me to drag me into the car'; 'generally only the first day or the first week'). S27 (2020) and S08 (2023 tech day 'exciting and scary') show the same pattern before 2022 and after. Points to a fear that is anticipatory and relieved by support and doing the work.
claims.alternative: Pre-show and first-day nerves are common among actors; 'nervous breakdown' is colloquial, not clinical, and must not be presented as a diagnosis. His journalist in S01 first assumed he was fishing for compliments; he insisted 'Genuine!'.

claims.claim: The café exchange: 'Do you really think so?'
claims.passage: Do you really think so?
claims.inference: Hattenstone's account of the exchange.
claims.alternative: Interviewer first assumed he was fishing for compliments.

claims.claim: The pre-job dread in his words.
claims.passage: this is the one where people will find me out, see that what's underneath the car bonnet doesn't work
claims.inference: Establishes what he said, to whom and when; it is a self-report, not proof of motive.
claims.alternative: "Nervous breakdown" is colloquial; the draft says so explicitly.

claims.claim: He insisted he meant it: 'Genuine!'
claims.passage: Genuine!
claims.inference: Journalist tested the claim and reports he said it "fiercely".
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Across a decade he has described the same doubt in the same shape: that he will be found out, that people really wanted someone else, or that each job is a mistake, even as the roles got bigger.
claims.passage: He has described the same doubt, in nearly the same shape, for a decade.
claims.inference: Dated statements: 2016 'If I never work again after this, Hamlet will be the role that ended my career' (S06); 2020 'always certain I'm gonna be terrible' (S27); 2021 'I still find it hard to sit down and say, wow, that was really good' (S10); 2022 'When are they going to realise that they really wanted the other guy?' (S02) and 'As long as people don't cotton on to my limitations' (S01); 2024 'imposter syndrome' from early on (S25) and 'Every time I get any job, I go: "Jesus, what? Really? Me?"' (S15). The repetition across outlets, interviewers and nine years is what makes it evidence of a pattern rather than a pose.
claims.alternative: British self-deprecation and press modesty can produce lines like these on demand; some are jokes. Against that, the S01 journalist tested it and he held to it, and he offers the same account on podcasts with friends (S24, S25).

claims.claim: 2016: 'If I never work again after this, Hamlet will be the role that ended my career.'
claims.passage: If I never work again after this, Hamlet will be the role that ended my career.
claims.inference: Establishes what he said, to whom and when; it is a self-report, not proof of motive.
claims.alternative: Wry; the draft says it "read as a joke".

claims.claim: 2020 livestream: four months of auditions, elation, then dread.
claims.passage: very, very stressed and anxious and nervous
claims.inference: Three transcriptions agree on the quoted words (medium.en, large-v3-turbo; captions agree on this phrase).
claims.alternative: Told to an old friend on a lockdown livestream.

claims.claim: 2020 stage-fright answer.
claims.passage: I've tricked so many people.
claims.inference: Quoted from the three-way transcript check; "gonna" follows captions and turbo.
claims.alternative: Partly comic; he immediately says the worry is "not a useful way" to spend energy, which the draft reports.

claims.claim: Finlay recalled Essiedu begging him not to see Pass Over before press night.
claims.passage: Finlay, for his part, recalled being begged not to come and see _Pass Over_ before press night.
claims.inference: Friend testimony, paraphrased.
claims.alternative: Based on the medium.en transcript only; Essiedu then thanked him for "going against my advice" (not quoted).

claims.claim: 2022 Soho House: 'When are they going to realise that they really wanted the other guy?'
claims.passage: When are they going to realise that they really wanted the other guy?
claims.inference: Establishes what he said, to whom and when; it is a self-report, not proof of motive.
claims.alternative: Jonathan Dean also wrote S04, so not a fully independent interviewer.

claims.claim: Dean's observation.
claims.passage: It does not sound like he is joking, either.
claims.inference: Interviewer's judgement.
claims.alternative: One interviewer's impression.

claims.claim: 2024: 'Every time I get any job, I go: "Jesus, what? Really? Me?"'
claims.passage: Every time I get any job, I go: 'Jesus, what? Really? Me?'
claims.inference: Establishes what he said, to whom and when; it is a self-report, not proof of motive.
claims.alternative: Original uses double quotes inside; the draft nests single quotes.

claims.claim: Being cast as Hamlet at 25 was, in his telling, the first time he truly doubted he could do something: seconds of elation followed by fear 'like a bucket of cold water', the figures of famous past Hamlets, and then doing it anyway, which taught him what was possible for him.
claims.passage: I don't know if I can do this. I don't know if I'm ready
claims.inference: Told in 2020 (S16, S27: four months of auditions 'very very stressed and anxious and nervous'), 2021 (S10), 2023 (S03) and 2024 (S25: 'I'm so scared ... can I even do this'). Shows the move from dread to action that recurs later (Delroy, Snape).
claims.alternative: Any 25-year-old in the RSC's first Black Hamlet would face real pressure, including press focus on race (S08, S05); the fear is circumstantially justified, so it shows his response more than his type.

claims.claim: He openly treats pessimism as insurance: expecting things to go wrong so that losing them hurts less, while calling that habit 'mad' and trying to change it.
claims.passage: If it all gets taken away, you don't feel that loss so keenly.
claims.inference: S01 follow-up call: 'If it all gets taken away, you don't feel that loss so keenly' and 'Perennially living in the expectation that things are going to fuck up is just mad. Even if it makes it feel quite sweet when they don't.' S07 (2024): 'The fear of things being taken away from you at any moment really kicks in'. S04 (2026): 'pretty sure I'm not going to be murdered… That could age badly!' This anticipatory bracing for loss is the closest thing in the record to a stated motive.
claims.alternative: Losing both parents by 20 and working in a precarious trade would teach anyone to brace for loss; a grief explanation competes with a temperament explanation and cannot be separated from it in public evidence.

claims.claim: The mezcal story: he called his work 'just a few little things' and asked 'what is wrong with me!'
claims.passage: And I thought: what is wrong with me!
claims.inference: Establishes what he said, to whom and when; it is a self-report, not proof of motive.
claims.alternative: Told against himself in a follow-up call.

claims.claim: He called the habit 'just mad'.
claims.passage: Perennially living in the expectation that things are going to fuck up is just mad.
claims.inference: He identifies the bracing and judges it.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: 2024 Mr Porter: fear of things being taken away.
claims.passage: The fear of things being taken away from you at any moment really kicks in
claims.inference: Context is his difficulty taking time off; his next sentence ("you need to respect your body...") is omitted in the cut draft.
claims.alternative: Fashion-retailer magazine.

claims.claim: He describes reading imagined verdicts on other people's faces: on a first day he sees 'What are you doing here?' in everyone's expression and knows he is projecting.
claims.passage: I read, 'What are you doing here?' on everybody's face.
claims.inference: One source, but a vivid first-person account of scanning others for threat and supplying the verdict himself. In Enneagram terms this resembles the projection associated with Type 6.
claims.alternative: Single-source. Social anxiety in a new group is widespread and not type-specific.

claims.claim: He knows he is projecting: 'somebody who is probably just having a cup of tea'; then 'Maybe they are thinking it.'
claims.passage: somebody who is probably just having a cup of tea
claims.inference: Establishes what he said, to whom and when; it is a self-report, not proof of motive.
claims.alternative: Single source.

claims.claim: 2023: he says he is thinking less about what people think of him.
claims.passage: right now I'm thinking less about what people might think about me
claims.inference: Counter-note to the doubt pattern; shows change.
claims.alternative: One interview; later statements (2024, 2025) show the doubt persisting.

claims.claim: Asked by a close friend whether he is preoccupied with being good and doing the right thing, he agreed and immediately explained his people-pleasing as an attempt to control how he is seen and 'to create safeness for yourself, safety for yourself', which he now weighs against being authentic.
claims.passage: trying to create safeness for yourself, safety for yourself
claims.inference: This is the most direct evidence on what his conscientiousness is for. He frames being good as a safety strategy rather than as meeting an inner standard of rightness (Type 1) or earning love (Type 2). The friend's question itself (Paloma Faith) is third-party testimony that he is visibly concerned with doing right.
claims.alternative: One podcast answer, given playfully and in therapy vocabulary he uses elsewhere; self-analysis can be a learned framing. It is still his explanation, unprompted, of his own behaviour.

claims.claim: Paloma Faith's question and his agreement.
claims.passage: I think you're very preoccupied about being good and doing the right thing all the time.
claims.inference: Friend testimony that he visibly cares about doing right; he answered "Yeah, totally."
claims.alternative: Playful framing by a friend and host.

claims.claim: He laughed because it was 'very front cortex at the moment for me'.
claims.passage: very front cortex at the moment for me
claims.inference: Indicates he was actively thinking about this at the time.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: He went on: 'Probably not' you can stay authentic; you must decide what matters more.
claims.passage: In the end, he suggested, you have to decide whether that matters more than letting your true self come out.
claims.inference: Paraphrase of the second half of his answer, included so the thesis quote is not cut off.
claims.alternative: Spoken in second person and therapy vocabulary.

claims.claim: As a drama student he was frightened of leaving the structure of training for an industry where the power lay with agents and casting directors, and co-founded a theatre company, Invertigo, to have something he could control.
claims.passage: I was really terrified about the feeling of having been in drama school and having a certain amount of stability within that structure
claims.inference: S27 (2020, audio) gives the motive; S06 (2016) confirms he set up Invertigo and says it helped him understand the industry. A security response to loss of structure: build your own structure.
claims.alternative: Many graduates start companies for creative agency or to get seen; his stated motive is the fear, but the action is common.

claims.claim: Invertigo motive continued.
claims.passage: I wanted to take control of my destiny
claims.inference: Three transcriptions agree.
claims.alternative: He also frames it as "artistic agency".

claims.claim: 'all the agency, all the power existed outside of me'.
claims.passage: it felt like all the agency, all the power existed outside of me
claims.inference: Three transcriptions agree.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: He repeatedly frames safety and trust as conditions for good work and urges young actors to find community: 'strength and security in numbers', being 'in safe hands', choosing a drama school where 'you feel safe' (S27), and keeping friends close because the industry can be very lonely.
claims.passage: You had to make sure that you were always in safe hands.
claims.inference: S13 (2020): 'Trust is a big word ... You had to make sure that you were always in safe hands'. S28 (2020, captions): 'strength and security in numbers'. S08 (2023): 'you can feel very alone. But I've found community and strength'. S25 (2024): advises young actors to 'cultivate a kind of feeling of community'. S10: friends and family 'the foundation of my life'.
claims.alternative: Safety and inclusion are also the explicit subject of these conversations (racism at drama school, intimate scenes), so the vocabulary is partly topic-driven, not only temperament.

claims.claim: Mountview advice (paraphrase).
claims.passage: to stick together in rooms that feel unsafe, because there is strength in numbers
claims.inference: Paraphrase of auto-caption text ("strength and security in numbers", "support each other").
claims.alternative: Captions only; no quotation used.

claims.claim: Big Issue 2023: community and strength.
claims.passage: But I've found community and strength, especially among people that have come from the same place as me.
claims.inference: Establishes what he said, to whom and when; it is a self-report, not proof of motive.
claims.alternative: Topic was solidarity during the 2023 strike.

claims.claim: Since 2016 he has said you cannot wear your heart on your sleeve all the time 'because people will take advantage'.
claims.passage: For anyone to survive, you cannot live with your heart on your sleeve all the time because people will take advantage
claims.inference: S06 (2016) and S10 (2021) in his own words; S08 (2023) 'savvy about the propensity of the industry to try and clip my wings'. Vigilance about others' intentions, consistent with a security-focused reading.
claims.alternative: As a working-class Black actor in a white-dominated industry, which has documented racism (S01, S38), wariness is realistic, not just temperament.

claims.claim: Michaela Coel, a friend since Guildhall, describes him as approaching characters 'almost with fear and trembling', egoless, 'very dependable' and 'always there in times of crisis'.
claims.passage: almost with fear and trembling
claims.inference: Independent named testimony from someone who has known him for over a decade and worked with him. Fear plus reliability plus loyalty is a recognisable cluster.
claims.alternative: A friend's tribute in a profile is warm by design. 'Fear and trembling' is a phrase about how he approaches characters, not his life generally.

claims.claim: Coel: 'he's always there in times of crisis'.
claims.passage: he's always there in times of crisis
claims.inference: Independent named testimony from a friend of more than a decade.
claims.alternative: A friend's tribute is warm by design.

claims.claim: Interpretation: leaning on others and being leaned on is one Six system.
claims.passage: In Six terms, that is one system: loyalty needed and loyalty given.
claims.inference: Draft's inference from C06 and C15.
claims.alternative: Dependability and reliance on friends are common to many types.

claims.claim: Colleagues consistently describe a playful, funny, unpretentious man under the seriousness: Jessie Buckley ('funny and naughty' with 'an ocean underneath'), Joe Barton ('gregarious', 'searing intelligence'), Lucy Prebble ('playful, brave and also technically brilliant'), Saoirse Ronan ('doesn't take himself too seriously').
claims.passage: He is funny, and colleagues tend to mention it first.
claims.inference: Several independent collaborators; S09 gathered Buckley, Barton, Prebble and Lennie James separately. Balances the anxious self-portrait with how he comes across in rooms.
claims.alternative: All are promotional contexts with co-workers; praise is expected. The humour itself fits several types.

claims.claim: Buckley: 'funny and naughty' 'with an ocean underneath'.
claims.passage: with an ocean underneath
claims.inference: Colleague testimony.
claims.alternative: Promotional setting.

type_hypothesis.against: A real case points elsewhere. He is conscientious to the point of self-punishment ('sadomasochistic self-flagellation', 'Tries his best', diligence, 'I do take my work seriously'), principled and political in his choices ('not the kind of person who puts his head in the sand'), and a close friend volunteers that he is 'very preoccupied about being good and doing the right thing all the time': that is Type 1 territory (C26, C27, C28, C11's question). Several Six markers are weaker than they look: impostor feelings and first-night nerves are near-universal among actors, British press modesty rewards self-deprecation, and losing both parents by 20 plus documented racism at drama school (C29) would make anyone brace for loss and watch for exploitation, so circumstance competes with temperament for C09 and C14. He also acts without seeking permission or protection when it matters: signing the trans-rights letter without advice during the Snape casting, refusing to report death threats, saying no to big projects (C19, C26). Other live notes: grief as a companion and sadness that makes people 'authentic, unique individuals' (Type 4, C23); a peacemaking, rarely angry stance and Coel's 'peaceful' (Type 9, C24); 'rescuing and fixing' and medicine as helping (Type 2, C33); restlessness, 'difficult to sit still', 'grass is always greener' (Type 7, C32); and a competitive overdrive that ran him into a medical tent (Type 3 or 8, C31).
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 1 explains his discipline, his inner critic and his moral seriousness directly: a mother who demanded he 'give it your all' and treat acting with a doctor's professionalism; obsessive preparation (warm-ups, shadowing rehearsals); rehearsal as being 'confronted by inadequacy'; difficulty calling his own work good; principled refusals of stereotyped roles and big commercial projects; anger reserved for rule-breakers and bigots (Johnson 'can get away with breaking the rules he made'); restrained personal anger he links to 'Christian guilt'; and a friend's unprompted read that he is preoccupied with being good. Type 4 is the next rival (grief kept close as identity, authenticity language, distinctive self-presentation), then 9 (peacemaker, steady, 'surrender to that') and 2 (helping, people-pleasing).
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What he says the vigilance and the goodness are for. When he explains his own conscientiousness he does not talk about getting it right or meeting a standard; he talks about safety and exposure. Asked directly whether he is preoccupied with being good, he answers that people-pleasing is 'an attempt to exert control ... trying to create safeness for yourself, safety for yourself' (S24, 2025). His self-criticism points outward to others' verdicts and to loss, not to an internal rule: 'this is the one where people will find me out', reading 'What are you doing here?' on every face (S01, 2022); 'When are they going to realise that they really wanted the other guy?' (S02, 2022); 'If it all gets taken away, you don't feel that loss so keenly' (S01); 'The fear of things being taken away from you at any moment' (S07, 2024); the same doubt in 2016, 2020, 2021 and 2024 (C07). He leans on people to get through it ('I need a lot of support from the people who are close to me to drag me into the car', S01) and builds structures when they disappear (Invertigo, C12), and his advice to others is trust, safe hands and 'strength and security in numbers' (C13). A One's critic says the work is not yet right and usually white-knuckles alone; his says he will be exposed and lose his place, and he seeks allies. His anger fits the same axis: it fires at people in authority who betray those in their care (C25), not at error in general. And when danger is real rather than anticipated he moves toward it and is steady (King Lear step-in, Hamlet, Delroy, Snape threats: C17, C18, C19), the counterphobic pattern of a Six rather than the reform impulse of a One. Against a Four: he postponed and boxed up grief for years rather than dwelling in it, refuses to use roles as therapy, and resists identity labels instead of cultivating distinctiveness (C22, C23).
